photos.description: Peperomia obtusifolia (Linnaeus, 1753) - baby rubber plant (Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation's Native Plant Nursery, Sanibel Island, Florida, USA) Plants are multicellular, photosynthesizing eucaryotes. Most species occupy terrestrial environments, but they also occur in freshwater and saltwater aquatic environments. The oldest known land plants in the fossil record are Ordovician to Silurian. Land plant body fossils are known in Silurian sedimentary rocks - they are small and simple plants (e.g., Cooksonia). Fossil root traces in paleosol horizons are known in the Ordovician. During the Devonian, the first trees and forests appeared. Earth's initial forestation event occurred during the Middle to Late Paleozoic. Earth's continents have been partly to mostly covered with forests ever since the Late Devonian. Occasional mass extinction events temporarily removed much of Earth's plant ecosystems - this occurred at the Permian-Triassic boundary (251 million years ago) and the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary (65 million years ago). The most conspicuous group of living plants is the angiosperms, the flowering plants. They first unambiguously appeared in the fossil record during the Cretaceous. They quickly dominated Earth's terrestrial ecosystems, and have dominated ever since. This domination was due to the evolutionary success of flowers, which are structures that greatly aid angiosperm reproduction. The baby rubber plant is reportedly native to parts of the subtropical and tropical New World - Florida, Central America, northern South America, and Caribbean area islands. Classification: Plantae, Angiospermophyta, Piperales, Piperaceae See info. at: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peperomia_obtusifolia

photos.description: The Oyster Plant (Tradescantia spathacea) is widely grown in the Philippines, where it thrives due to the tropical climate. It is commonly used as an ornamental ground cover in gardens, landscaping projects, and even as a houseplant because of its vibrant purple and green foliage. Growing the Oyster Plant in the Philippines: Climate: The warm and humid conditions of the Philippines are ideal for this plant, as it mimics its native tropical habitat. Location: It grows well outdoors in partial shade or full sun. Indoors, place it near a window where it gets bright, indirect light. Soil: Use well-draining soil to avoid waterlogging, which can lead to root rot, especially during the rainy season. Watering: Water moderately. During hot seasons, water more frequently, but ensure the soil isn't waterlogged. Maintenance: Trim dead or yellowing leaves to keep the plant healthy and attractive. Fertilize lightly during the growing season (spring to early rainy season). Propagation: Propagation is easy through division or stem cuttings. Simply replant sections with roots or stems in moist soil. Caution: While the Oyster Plant is beautiful and hardy, its sap can irritate the skin and eyes. Additionally, it is mildly toxic if ingested, so keep it out of reach of children and pets.

I don't speak of photography techniques in the notes I post with most of my photos. I will make an exception this time. The DxO Film Pack contains a preset that attempts to replicate Kodak Elite slide film processed with Kodak print negative developer. The result emphasizes greens and yellows and sometimes makes the preset the best one for photos of plants with yellow flowers and large green leaves. In most other instances, it creates a false-color image that exaggerates greens and yellows tremendously. I chose it for this photo for I wanted to attract viewers attention to the reproductive parts ot the flower.. See the photo to the right for a more accurate rendition.
